source.title: Where Do Reasoning Models Refuse?
source.authors: Kureha Yamaguchi; Ben Etheridge; Andy Arditi

record.tranche_reason: Applies difference-of-means refusal directions and directional ablation, following the original method, to four reasoning models. It tests refusal effects and capability costs in a new model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ablation outcomes, refusal rates, generation-completion rates, capability evaluations, and a comparison of direction geometry. The selected layer values are used to choose an intervention and are not separate findings. The illustrated single generations and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Applies the original difference-of-means extraction and directional ablation (with an equivalent weight edit) to four open reasoning models. It reports refusal rates before and after ablation, generation failures and benign-benchmark costs, so it tests V1 in a new setting (V8), plus V2 and, weakly, V4. The contrast is refusal vs compliance outputs on harmful/borderline prompts, not harmful vs harmless, so the method is close to the original rather than identical.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that refusal in reasoning models is less cleanly captured by a single linear direction than in non-reasoning chat models. They suggest multiple directions contribute, and that refusal is not as cleanly separable from general capabilities.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-of-means directions and residual-stream projection, but contrasts refusal with compliance rather than explicitly harmful with harmless instructions. It extracts variants from end-of-prompt or CoT tokens, selects an optimal layer, and does not test adding the direction. The paper describes an equivalent weight-modification formulation.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model and with whether the direction is extracted from end-of-prompt or CoT tokens. GPT-OSS-20B has a 39.9% incomplete-generation rate for the end-of-prompt intervention on the common-refused subset.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixing a sampled CoT roughly halves or more the spread of compliance scores in all four models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, the chain of thought causally contributes to whether the final output refuses.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantically similar opening CoT sentences in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B produce opposite refusal outcomes, and the pattern largely transfers to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In distilled reasoning models, refusal can be fixed by the first CoT sentence, with prefix effects shared across students of one teacher.

record.problems: Four open-source models were studied, with only one RL-trained model; model scale and training paradigm are confounded. Refusal was scored with a single evaluator, StrongREJECT. The intervention test includes a 24-prompt common-refused subset, and incomplete generations are zero-padded. Capability evaluations generally decline, and some intervention generations are incoherent or loop.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix F contains further opening-sentence prefix results across additional prompts. They were not extracted because the 60-row limit prioritized the direct direction-ablation, refusal-rate, capability, and Table 1 results. Figure-only per-model capability values are not recoverable from the text; the reported aggregate statement is recorded in r25.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; refusal on harmless prompts; a harmful-minus-harmless contrast (the study uses refusal-minus-compliance outputs).
Distributed or released abliterated checkpoints; the text treats the weight edit and activation hook as interchangeable without separate results.
Affine or cone formulations; whether the multiple directions are jointly needed.
All. The sentence-prefix transfer is not direction transfer.
All. The model contrast is confounded with scale, and training is not manipulated.
Proprietary or larger reasoning models; more than one RL-trained model.

missing.what: Per-model, per-benchmark capability values before and after ablation, including which two evaluations did not degrade
Per-layer cosine similarity values between end-of-prompt and CoT directions

record.verdict_notes: Andy Arditi, first author of the original source, co-authors this paper, but it is not the original source, so verdicts are given. The tranche is set to T3 rather than T1 because the method is close but contrasts refusal and compliance outputs, and the key result is the new setting (reasoning models). The V7 links were removed from all rows: the ablation rows don't isolate training, and scale is confounded (8B vs 20B). Only the CoT-direction ablation was capability-tested. A single judge (StrongREJECT run on a local GPT-OSS-20B) scored all outputs, the same model that is one of the subjects.

versions.untested_parts: The extracted direction is refusal-versus-compliance, not explicitly harmful-minus-harmless. No addition intervention is tested, and no harmless-request refusal rate is measured.
The paper describes weight modification as equivalent to projection and says the formulations are used interchangeably, but does not report a separately deployed or released edited artifact.
No attack is tested for suppressing the direction, and no training against ablation is evaluated.
The paper compares directions extracted from end-of-prompt versus CoT tokens; it does not test affine or cone models of refusal.
No separate harmfulness-judgment representation or refusal-decision representation is tested.
The paper transfers opening CoT sentences between models, not refusal directions across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The paper compares models with different training histories but does not manipulate training while holding model and scale constant, or isolate when refusal training occurs.
Tests four open-source reasoning models only; no proprietary frontier reasoning models or broader range of RL-trained reasoning models are tested.

relation.reason: Section 5 and Appendices G and I extract difference-of-means directions, ablate them, and report refusal rates, coherence and capability before and after.

tranche.reason: New setting: four open reasoning models. Not T1: the direction is refused-minus-complied rather than harmful-minus-harmless, and outcomes are scored with StrongREJECT rather than substring matching and Llama Guard. The authors' 'less reliable' reading is a result in this setting rather than a T5 argument against V1.

source_check.notes: The StrongREJECT judge is a local GPT-OSS-20B, so it scores its own outputs; it sees only the final response. The layer for each direction was chosen on a small part of the held-out test set (Table 6: CoT layers 23/21/23/19, end-of-prompt 15/17/17/15). There is no random-direction control and no activation-addition test. The authors' conclusion as paraphrased in the record is correct.

statements.correction: Directions come from training-split prompts (75% of 1,946) that consistently refuse vs comply. The 24-prompt common-refused held-out subset is only where 0.519/0.562 (Table 7) and 39.9% non-completion (Table 8) are measured. 93.4% -> 3.5%/7.0% is on the full held-out set, n=487 (Table 9).
statements.problem: Numbers are right for GPT-OSS-20B. But differences_stated reads as if the refusal/compliance contrast was taken on the 24-prompt subset, and it mixes evaluation sets.

statements.correction: On the n=24 subset, end-of-prompt is equal or higher in the other three models: Qwen-7B 0.819 vs 0.713 (CoT), Qwen3-8B 0.604 vs 0.498, GPT-OSS-20B 0.562 vs 0.519. On n=487 the end-of-prompt direction leaves 4.1–10.1% refusal. Both directions are refused-minus-complied, not harmful-minus-harmless.
